turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Grab a seat. What's been going on?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning. It's the diabetes, that's the main thing. The sugars have been all over the shop, and I'm waking up thirsty, proper thirsty, and then I'm up in the night for a wee. I kept thinking it'd settle and it hasn't, so here I am.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thirsty, and up passing urine. How long's that been?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't put a proper date on it. It was since Diwali, or after Diwali, one of the two. The sweets were out and I was already refilling the water bottle, but whether it kicked off that week or a bit later I honestly couldn't tell you.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): So around Diwali, exact start unclear. The night-time wees the same period?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, same stretch. Twice a night, sometimes three if I've had a late cup of tea, which I know is my own fault. I do accounts at the council, early starts, so the broken sleep wrecks the next morning, but that's the job as much as anything.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any tiredness with it, or a change in your weight?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Tired, yes. Wiped out by the arvo, most work days. Weekends I sleep in and I'm better, so I don't reckon it's my mood, I still yell at the cricket. Weight, I don't think so, the trousers fit the same, and the scales are in the laundry which I walk past and forget.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your eyes? Blurring, floaters, trouble with the screen?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, eyes are fine. I can read the spreadsheet without squinting. I did see the optometrist, but that was last winter, or the one before, I get those mixed up. They reckoned the back of the eye looked alright, as far as I remember.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Worth knowing, even with the date fuzzy. Feet now. Any numbness, tingling, sores?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Tingling, yeah, pins and needles in both feet, mostly the toes, worse when I'm stuck at the desk. No sores, and no pain really, just that fizzing. My wife usually makes me look, actually I look myself, she's at her sister's in Geelong. It started last winter, or maybe the winter before that, and I can't lock it down.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tingling in both feet for about a winter or two, no sores, no real pain. I'll examine them shortly. Can you run me through the medicines?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin, the big tablets, a thousand milligrams morning and night, with food. Years I've been on that. And the Lantus at night, the insulin pen, which is the one that gets messy.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): The practice nurse's note from last time has Lantus at twenty-four units at bedtime. Is that what you dial up?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I do eighteen. She wrote twenty-four, I think because she wanted me to increase, we had a yarn about it, but I never moved the dial. Eighteen units, on the nights I actually take it, and I'm sure about the eighteen.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): So you inject eighteen, and the file says twenty-four. I won't pretend those match. Do you get it in every night?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Not if I'm honest. On work days with a six o'clock start I'm on the train before five, and I skip it, because I don't want to go low in the carriage. Three nights a week, sometimes four. Weekends I take it every time.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the bedtime insulin is missed on those early shifts. Anything else you've had for the sugar?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Gliclazide. I stopped it in March. About an hour after breakfast I'd get the shakes and the sweats, proper hypo feelings, so I rang here and they said stop, and I stopped. Haven't touched a tablet of it since.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stopped in March after those hypo symptoms. None of that since you came off it?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No shakes since. And, um, they also printed a script for Jardiance, the flozin tablet, but I never took it. The box is still in the drawer. I read about urine infections and I just didn't start.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, I won't list Jardiance as something you're on. What numbers have you actually seen on the meter?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting, before breakfast, it's one-eighty-something. Sometimes I think one-ninety, sometimes one-seven-something, the screen's tiny and I don't always write it in the book. I don't even know if that's the milligram setting. The meter was my brother's, from when he lived in the States.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): So a muddled fasting figure, somewhere around one-eighty, and the unit isn't clear. I can't treat that as a real result. Do you check later in the day?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): After dinner it's higher, I reckon, but I don't test then. I get in late, the pen and the meter are in the bedroom, and I'm already half asleep. Sorry, I'm giving you the long version of everything.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're fine. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, swelling in the ankles?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none of that. Breathing's good. Ankles look normal. I checked this morning because I thought you might ask.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of. Not penicillin, not anything.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll do your blood pressure and have a look at the feet. Socks off when you're ready.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep. The left one always sticks on the heel. There you go.

[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is one hundred and thirty-six over eighty-two. Pulse is seventy-eight. Both feet are warm, the pulses are there, the skin's intact with no ulcers, and the monofilament is reduced over the toes.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Reduced. I thought I felt a couple of the pokes. Maybe I was guessing on the toes.

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): You did feel some of them. The toe sites were down. Let me say it back so we're on the same page. Known type 2 diabetes, thirst and night wees since around Diwali that you can't date, foot tingling since last winter or the one before, metformin a thousand milligrams twice a day, Lantus eighteen on your dial or twenty-four in the nurse's note, skipped on early shifts, gliclazide off since March, and Jardiance never started.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the lot, yeah. The eighteen is what actually goes in, whatever the note says.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is the type 2 diabetes is not well controlled, given the thirst and the overnight wees. The foot tingling may be early neuropathy. Neither of those is a final diagnosis today.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. I knew the skipping wasn't clever. It's just the train, and picturing myself on the floor of the carriage.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. Stay on the metformin, one thousand milligrams twice a day with food, and that includes work mornings. For the insulin, don't skip it, but keep dialling eighteen units at night rather than twenty-four until the bloods are back. If you're anxious about the early train, have a small snack with the injection instead of leaving it out.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Eighteen, not twenty-four, and take it even when the alarm's at five. A muesli bar if I'm nervous, not a whole production. I can do that.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. I'll organise an HbA1c, kidney function, and a urine albumin, this week if you can get to the lab.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday before work is free. Is the urine one just the little jar they hand you?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, the lab gives you the jar. I'd also like the eye screening service to see you, because we can't date that optometrist visit. I'll put that referral through.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. And the feet, day to day, what do I actually do?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Look at them every day, moisturise, and don't walk around barefoot. If the skin breaks, come in that day, not next month.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Daily look, cream, shoes on. What about coming back here?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Book a follow-up in four weeks. If the sugars feel like they're climbing fast, or the shakes come back, come earlier and don't sit on it.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks, and earlier if I feel crook. Should I bring the meter, and the pen so you can see the dial?
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Bring the meter, a written list of readings if you can manage it, and the Lantus box. Leave the gliclazide stopped. We are not restarting it today.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Box by the door, next to the keys, that's the only system that works for me. I do the same thing with my lunch. The gliclazide can stay in the cupboard.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the tiredness, weekends you're yourself and you're still enjoying things, so I'll note it with the sugars rather than as a mood problem.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Weekends I'm fine. I know I over-explain, my daughter pulls me up on it.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): You filled in the gaps I needed. I'll see you in four weeks, sooner if it slides.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Thanks. I'll try not to skip. Thursday for the bloods, yeah?
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thursday is fine.

omissions.text: Lantus dose is incompletely recorded under medications: the patient said he actually injects 18 units at night, while the nurse note said 24 units; this is a real discrepancy and the actual current dose is 18 units.
The patient misses Lantus on early-shift work days, about 3 nights a week and sometimes 4, because he is worried about going low on the train; weekends he takes it every time.
Gliclazide was stopped because about an hour after breakfast it caused shakes and sweats suggestive of hypoglycaemia, and those symptoms resolved after stopping.
Jardiance (the 'flozin' tablet) had been prescribed/dispensed but was never started; the box is still in the drawer because the patient was worried about urine infections.

The fasting glucose readings are not reliable/interpretable: the patient reported 'one-eighty-something' or sometimes 190 or 170-something, did not record them consistently, and the meter may be using mg/dL because it came from his brother in the United States; the doctor said he could not treat this as a real result.
Negative finding missing: no numbness in the feet was elicited when asked about 'numbness, tingling, sores'.
The patient reported no known medication allergies, specifically including no penicillin allergy.

Previous eye check detail missing/wrongly simplified: the patient said he saw an optometrist last winter or the winter before and, as far as he remembered, they said the back of the eye looked alright.
Follow-up red flag advice missing: if the skin on the feet breaks, he should come in that day, not next month.
